part1.text: Every enterprise has built this pilot. An AI that reads every policy in seconds… and acts on none of them.
So the employee closes the chat, logs into three portals, and does the work by hand. The human is still the copy-paste bus.
Enterprise AI moves through four stages. The real chasm is between an agent that acts with shared keys, and one that acts under governance.
The rule is simple. The model proposes. Deterministic services decide. The model never holds a credential, and never grades its own permissions.
Between a sentence and a system of record, there are nine gates: identity, policy, approval, a signed one-time grant, and a tamper-evident audit trail.
Same assistant, three requests. A leave request executes. A salary change is blocked by policy. A poisoned spreadsheet never gets a grant.
And friction scales with blast radius. Not every action needs a human. Some need two.

part2.text: Would you give your ERP keys to software that one sentence in a PDF can reprogram? No CISO would. Yet that's how most AI agents are wired.
Hide one instruction in row forty-two of a vendor spreadsheet, and a naive agent changes the bank details. No firewall was breached. It just read a poisoned row.
System prompts are advice, not security boundaries. That's authorization in client-side JavaScript.
And your API gateway approves four failures it can't see: prompt injection, the confused deputy, retry amplification, and tool drift.
So assume the model will be tricked, and contain it anyway, behind five trust boundaries.
Run the same poisoned file through a governed pipeline. It's filtered, delimited, and denied by policy. Zero execution grants. Nothing reaches the ERP.
Four rules before any agent gets write access: no ambient authority, no model-filled identity, no blind retries, and no dispatch without a signed grant.

part3.text: Every department is building its own AI. Each with its own prompts, guardrails, and logs.
Five assistants, five guardrail schemes, five audit formats, and not one shared kill switch. It's the integration mess of the two-thousands, all over again.
Governance should never live inside the application. Capabilities should be governed contracts, not code.

Whether a system speaks OpenAPI, MCP, or a native SDK, it becomes one canonical contract, with a risk tier, hidden identity fields, and a pinned hash. The model plans against the contract, never the raw endpoint.
Nothing reaches production by default. A connector exposes a hundred and forty operations. All are quarantined. Only twelve make it through review and certification.
And when a tool changes overnight, its hash no longer matches. The new version is quarantined, while the live one keeps serving.
Govern once. Connect everything. One policy engine, one audit trail, one kill switch.

part4.text: In a demo, an AI agent is a simple loop. Call the model, call a tool, repeat. In a system of record, that loop is a disaster waiting to happen.
Step two waits four hours for approval. Step three times out after the payment was sent. A restart wipes the state, and a blind retry pays twice.
So split the work between two engines. A bounded planner owns the reasoning. A durable workflow engine owns execution, approvals, and retries.
The planner runs a fixed ten-stage graph, with hard caps: six nodes, three writes, one write at a time, and a single repair attempt.
A request becomes a typed plan. Reads run in parallel. The write waits for its precondition, and checks the record has not changed underneath it.
And if the network times out after dispatch, nothing retries blindly. The operation is quarantined, then reconciled by its idempotency key.

part5.text: Most systems check permissions once, at login. For an AI agent, that is nowhere near enough.
Between the prompt and the API call, it searches, plans, and may wait hours for approval. With a shared service token, it becomes a confused deputy, with more power than the person who asked.
Its real authority is an intersection: the signed-in user, the assistant’s ceiling, live ownership of the record, and a single-use grant.
So authorization runs continuously, across seven checkpoints, from the session to the millisecond of execution.
The model never sees identity fields. Tools are filtered by policy before it ranks them. And retrieval runs on sixty-second signed scopes.
Change four days to fourteen after approval, and the grant’s digest no longer matches. Dispatch stops before a single secret is fetched.

part6.text: When teams realise autonomous actions are risky, they add a confirm button to everything.
It fails twice. People approve twenty times a day without reading. And the person who typed the prompt is not the person who should authorize a payroll change.
So friction should follow blast radius. Five risk tiers, from autonomous reads to actions the model may never take.
Context escalates the tier: restricted data, more than ten records, or an irreversible change. The most restrictive rule always wins.
An approval becomes a cryptographic commitment: a deterministic preview, a plan hash, a single-use nonce, and fresh multi-factor proof.
For high-risk actions, the requester can never be the final approver. Two people. One exact payload.

part7.text: Six months after launch, internal audit asks one question. Who changed vendor record eighty-eight twenty-one, and why?
They want the prompt, the evidence, the policy version, the approval, the grant, and the receipt. And proof that none of it was altered.
Logs tell engineers a service is healthy. They do not prove who authorized what.
So every run carries seventeen correlated identifiers, from the user’s turn to the external system’s receipt.
Each event is hash-chained to the one before it. Change a single byte, and the chain breaks against a signed, immutable anchor.
And every audience sees a different projection. The model gets the minimum. The auditor gets the record.

part8.text: Every board eventually asks two questions. How do we roll this out safely? And how fast can we stop it?
Never jump from a pilot to high-risk writes. Adoption moves through five rings, from shadow mode to four-eyes regulated operations.
Every rollout ring is guarded by release gates, from contract certification to load and penetration testing.
And four independent kill switches. Freeze all writes, hold high-risk actions, isolate one connector, or pause schedules, while knowledge answers keep running.
Configuration ships as signed, versioned bundles, diffed and simulated before promotion.
The future of enterprise AI is not more access. It is the right capabilities, within the right boundaries, under the right governance.
